planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed, in blocks of at least four short rows for reliable pollination.

directions: This long-popular bicolor normal-sugary (SU) hybrid produces two ears per stalk with kernels randomly mixed between golden yellow and creamy white, giving each cob a distinctive speckled look on the plate. Because it is a standard SU type rather than a supersweet, it does not need to be isolated from other sugary corns and holds its eating quality on the stalk for several days past peak, giving gardeners a wider harvest window. Keep plants well watered from tasseling through ear fill, since drought stress at that stage is the most common cause of poorly filled tips. It remains a favorite roadside-stand and home-garden choice for gardeners who want classic old-fashioned corn flavor rather than the extra crunch of newer sh2 hybrids.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks after the soil is thoroughly warm, allowing the full season needed for kernels to dry down on the stalk.

directions: Mandan Bride is an heirloom flour corn attributed to the Mandan people of the upper Missouri River, grown historically alongside beans and squash in traditional Three Sisters plantings. Each ear carries an unpredictable mix of red, orange, black, yellow, and white kernels, and because the whole kernel is soft and starchy rather than hard-hulled like flint corn, it grinds easily into flour once fully dried. Leave ears on the stalk until husks are papery and kernels are rock-hard before harvesting, then cure indoors for several weeks in a well-ventilated spot before grinding or storing. Beyond its culinary use, gardeners often grow it for its striking multicolored ears, which make excellent autumn braids and decorations.

planting.note: Wait until soil has warmed well above 65 degrees F before direct sowing, since this tender-hulled hybrid germinates poorly in cold, wet ground.

directions: Bred in Japan and marketed under the Mirai trademark, this bicolor hybrid is prized for exceptionally thin, tender pericarps and very high sugar content that many gardeners describe as fruit-like sweetness eaten raw off the cob. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil and give it consistent moisture through silking, since the thin-walled kernels are more sensitive to stress cracking than standard sh2 supersweets. Ears fill out to the tip reliably with 7 to 8 inch cobs on sturdy stalks, and the variety holds refrigerated quality in the husk for up to two weeks, longer than most sweet corn. Choose this cultivar when the priority is the sweetest possible fresh-eating experience rather than maximum yield or field storability.

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks well after last frost and isolate from other corn types by distance or timing to keep popping quality true.

directions: Maintained for generations among Pennsylvania Dutch growers, Amish Butter is a pre-1885 heirloom popcorn that produces tall, dark-green stalks topped with two conical ears carrying a mix of rice- and pearl-shaped ivory-white kernels. Let ears dry fully on the stalk, or finish drying them indoors on their husks, until kernels rattle loosely in the cob before shelling and storing in a breathable container. Because the kernels are soft enough to also grind for flour, hominy, or polenta, gardeners get a genuinely dual-purpose corn from a single planting rather than a popcorn-only crop. The fluffy white pop and rich, naturally buttery flavor are the main reasons collectors keep this variety in circulation.

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks after danger of frost has passed; plant alongside another sugary-enhanced variety to improve pollination and kernel fill.

directions: Ruby Queen is a sugary-enhanced hybrid grown as much for its deep ruby-red kernels as for its old-fashioned corn flavor, with 8 inch ears carrying 16 to 18 rows on 7-foot stalks. Harvest at the blush stage for the sweetest eating, or let ears ripen further to full red for a richer, more traditional corn taste; steam, grill, or microwave rather than boil to keep the color from fading into the cooking water. The red tassels and husks make the standing plants attractive in the garden and useful for fall decorating even before the ears are picked. Choose it when a gardener wants a novelty-colored sweet corn that still delivers genuinely good fresh eating rather than an ornamental-only variety.

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks well after last frost and isolate from other corn by distance or staggered timing to protect popping quality and kernel color.

directions: Shaman's Blue was the first widely offered dark-blue hybrid popcorn, bred for large, tender kernels that pop bright white despite their deep bluish-purple hull color, unlike the small, chewy kernels typical of older open-pollinated blue popcorns. Leave 8 inch ears on the stalk until husks are fully dry and kernels are hard, then cure indoors before shelling and storing in a sealed container to preserve popping moisture. The anthocyanin-rich hull gives raw kernels a deeper color than yellow popcorns, which growers selling at farmers markets often use as a selling point alongside its reliably fluffy pop. Choose this variety when a gardener wants the visual novelty of blue corn without sacrificing tender, large-kernel popping performance.
